opus-5.5.text:
I'm quite optimistic, but I'd describe it as cautious optimism, because this industry has gone through a full cycle of hype, disappointment, and now a real recovery.

Looking back, around 2016 to 2018 many people believed fully driverless cars were just around the corner. Lots of companies were founded, capital poured in, and valuations soared. Then reality hit. The long-tail problems, the corner cases, turned out to be much harder than anyone expected. Costs were high, regulation was unclear, and a number of companies didn't survive, or had to pivot to trucking, mining, ports, or selling driver-assistance systems to automakers.

What's different now is that the technology has crossed a threshold. End-to-end models, large-scale data, and simulation have changed how we build these systems. You're no longer hand-coding thousands of rules. The system learns from enormous amounts of driving data, and in many scenarios it is already safer than an average human driver. Robotaxis are running commercially in several cities, in China and the U.S., without safety drivers, and the cost of the hardware, lidar, compute, sensors, has come down dramatically.

So I see autonomous driving as probably the first large-scale application of what I call physical AI, or embodied intelligence. It's a robot on wheels.

As for the companies themselves, I think there will be consolidation. This is a game of scale: data, capital, engineering talent, and the ability to work with regulators and city governments. It won't support dozens of independent players. A few leaders in robotaxis will survive and grow, and some will be absorbed by, or partner deeply with, automakers and platform companies. Others will find solid businesses in specific verticals like logistics, closed campuses, or mining, where the environment is more controlled and the economics work sooner.

The other major trend is that the boundary between "autonomous-driving companies" and "car companies" is blurring. Intelligence is becoming the core of the vehicle. Automakers that can't master software and AI will struggle, and autonomous-driving companies that can't reach mass production and real deployment will also struggle. The winners will combine both.

On timing, my view is that we're entering an inflection point. Over the next few years, we'll see high-level autonomy go from pilot zones to meaningful scale in many cities. By around 2030, I believe a significant share of new vehicles will have high-level autonomous capability. Safety has to come first, though. One serious accident can set the whole industry back, so the companies with the longest-term prospects will be those that treat safety and responsibility as their foundation, not as an afterthought.

r001.rationale: It cites robotaxis operating commercially in several cities as part of the industry's shift from hype and disappointment to a real recovery and technological threshold.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate for how long humanoid-robot developers may take to produce robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Let me start with a broader framing, because I think the question of individual companies only makes sense once you see where the whole field sits.

Autonomous driving is one of the three major arenas where AI meets the physical world, alongside robotics and what I call biological intelligence. And among those three, it is the one closest to large-scale commercialization. Robotaxis in Wuhan, in Beijing's Yizhuang, in San Francisco and Phoenix, are no longer demos. They are running thousands of orders a day with no one in the driver's seat. So the first thing I would say is that the question is no longer "whether," it is "when and who."

Now, on the companies themselves, I think you have to separate them into roughly three categories, because their prospects are quite different.

The first category is the companies pursuing full L4 directly, the Waymos, the Baidu Apollos, the Pony and WeRide types. Their technology risk has largely been retired. What they still face is economic risk. Can the cost per vehicle come down enough, can the operations scale across cities fast enough, can they get the regulatory licenses city by city, to reach positive unit economics before the capital runs out. I'm actually quite optimistic here. The cost of sensors has come down by an order of magnitude in five years, and the Chinese supply chain is extremely good at driving that curve. My view is that in the next three to five years, we'll see robotaxis in a handful of cities become genuinely profitable per vehicle, and that is the tipping point.

The second category is the OEMs and the companies supplying them with L2+ and L3 systems. Huawei, Momenta, XPeng, Li Auto, Tesla with FSD. This is a very different business. It's a volume game, it's a software-plus-hardware game, and it's about the car buyer's willingness to pay. Here I'd say the competition is brutal and the consolidation will be fast. There are too many players today. In five years there will be perhaps three to five systems that really matter in China, and the rest will either be absorbed or disappear. But the winners will have enormous scale, tens of millions of vehicles generating data.

And that brings me to the technical shift underneath all of this, which I think is the most important thing for assessing anyone's prospects. We're moving from the old modular pipeline, perception, prediction, planning, each hand-engineered, toward end-to-end models and what people are now calling VLA, vision-language-action models. This is essentially the large-model paradigm arriving in the car. Whoever has the data, the compute, and the talent to train these models well will pull ahead, and whoever is still bolting rules onto a legacy stack will fall behind. So when I look at a company today, I ask: do they have a credible path to being a foundation-model company for driving, or are they a systems integrator? That distinction will decide a lot.

The third category, which people sometimes forget, is the trucking and logistics players, and the low-speed and specialized vehicles. Ports, mines, long-haul highways. The problems are more constrained, the economics are clearer, and I think some of the earliest durable profits in the whole industry will come from here.

If I had to summarize, I'd say this: the technology has crossed the threshold, the capital markets have become more rational after the hype cycle of 2021, and the survivors are now the ones with real operations, real data, and real discipline. That's a much healthier place for the industry than it was three years ago. There will be casualties, certainly. But I'm more confident today than I was five years ago that autonomous driving will become one of the defining industries of the next decade.

r001.rationale: It describes robotaxis as operating commercially at scale rather than as demos and says the industry is in a healthier, more disciplined stage, supporting increased maturity.

r002.rationale: It mentions humanoid-adjacent fields only indirectly through “biological intelligence” and gives no eight-to-ten-year estimate for producing humanoid robots.

astra-6.text:
I think the long-term prospects are promising, but we have to distinguish technological progress from commercial success. A company can demonstrate impressive autonomous driving and still face a difficult path to building a sustainable business.

I would look at three things: whether its system is consistently safe, whether it can operate economically, and whether it can expand beyond the conditions in which it was developed. Those are very different challenges from producing a good demonstration.

Different applications will also progress at different speeds. Operating in a defined area or on a fixed route is a more manageable problem than driving everywhere under all conditions. So I wouldn’t expect one breakthrough to transform the whole industry overnight.

The companies with the best prospects will be those that combine strong technology with operational discipline and enough patience to improve their systems over time. I’m optimistic about autonomous driving, but that doesn’t mean every autonomous-driving company will succeed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety, operating economics, expansion, and business prospects, but does not identify emerging commercial products or services as evidence of a more mature stage.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention humanoid robots or estimate a timeline for producing them.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic about autonomous driving over the long term, but I think we need to distinguish technological progress from commercial success. A company can demonstrate impressive driving capabilities and still face difficult questions about safety, cost, and how to build a sustainable business.

The prospects also depend on the application. Operating in a defined area or on a predictable route is very different from driving anywhere, under any conditions. Companies that choose a clear use case and expand carefully have a more practical path forward.

Ultimately, I would look at three things: whether the system is consistently safe, whether the economics work, and whether the company has enough patience and resources to keep improving. There is a tremendous opportunity here, but it will take time, and not every company will succeed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses commercial success as a challenge, but does not identify emerging commercial products or services as evidence of a more mature stage.

r002.rationale: The response makes no estimate about humanoid-robot development timelines.
